claim: Efferent octopaminergic neurons projecting to the ovary are essential for germline stem cell (GSC) increase in response to mating in female Drosophila.
source: Here we report that efferent octopaminergic neurons projecting to the ovary are essential for germline stem cell (GSC) increase in response to mating in female Drosophila.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript including RNAi knockdown of octopamine biosynthesis genes and neuronal activation experiments.

claim: The neuronal activity of octopaminergic neurons is required for mating-induced GSC increase.
source: The neuronal activity of the octopaminergic neurons is required for mating-induced GSC increase as they relay the mating signal from sex peptide receptor-positive cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by experiments using TrpA1 activation and TNT inactivation of dsx+ Tdc2+ neurons shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: Octopaminergic neurons relay the mating signal from sex peptide receptor-positive cholinergic neurons.
source: The neuronal activity of the octopaminergic neurons is required for mating-induced GSC increase as they relay the mating signal from sex peptide receptor-positive cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by GRASP analysis showing physical connection between SPSNs and Tdc2+ neurons (Figure 6A) and genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 6E-F).

claim: Octopamine and its receptor Oamb are required for mating-induced GSC increase via intracellular Ca2+ signaling.
source: Octopamine and its receptor Oamb are also required for mating-induced GSC increase via intracellular Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through Oamb RNAi experiments (Figure 1C-D), calcium imaging with GCaMP6s (Figure 2D-E), and Insp3R manipulation experiments (Figure 2J).

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase-2 is a downstream component of the octopamine-Ca2+ signaling to induce GSC increase.
source: Moreover, we identified Matrix metalloproteinase-2 as a downstream component of the octopamine-Ca2+ signaling to induce GSC increase.
evidence: Supported by Mmp2 RNAi experiments showing impaired mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 4A) and epistasis experiments (Figure 4E).

claim: Mated females show a dramatic increase in egg production and GSC number.
source: Mated females show a dramatic increase in egg production, as well as GSC, which is induced by a male-derived peptide from the seminal fluid called sex peptide (SP) (Kubli, 2003; Yoshinari et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kubli, 2003; Yoshinari et al., 2019) and confirmed by data in Figure 1C showing increased GSC numbers in mated vs virgin females.

claim: Sex peptide (SP) is a male-derived peptide from seminal fluid that induces GSC increase.
source: Mated females show a dramatic increase in egg production, as well as GSC, which is induced by a male-derived peptide from the seminal fluid called sex peptide (SP) (Kubli, 2003; Yoshinari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature (Kubli, 2003; Yoshinari et al., 2019).

claim: SP is received by its specific receptor, sex peptide receptor (SPR), in a small subset of SPR-positive sensory neurons (SPSNs) located in the uterine lumen.
source: SP is received by its specific receptor, sex peptide receptor (SPR), in a small subset of SPR-positive sensory neurons (SPSNs), which are located in the uterine lumen and send afferent axons into the tip of the abdominal ganglion (Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Yapici et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Yapici et al., 2008).

claim: SPSNs send afferent axons into the tip of the abdominal ganglion.
source: SP is received by its specific receptor, sex peptide receptor (SPR), in a small subset of SPR-positive sensory neurons (SPSNs), which are located in the uterine lumen and send afferent axons into the tip of the abdominal ganglion (Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Yapici et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Yapici et al., 2008).

claim: SP-SPR signaling in SPSNs stimulates the biosynthesis of ovarian insect steroid hormones (ecdysteroids).
source: The SP-SPR signaling in the SPSNs stimulates the biosynthesis of the ovarian insect steroid hormones (ecdysteroids), which play an essential role in mating-induced GSC increase (Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016; Uryu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016; Uryu et al., 2015).

claim: Ecdysteroids play an essential role in mating-induced GSC increase.
source: The SP-SPR signaling in the SPSNs stimulates the biosynthesis of the ovarian insect steroid hormones (ecdysteroids), which play an essential role in mating-induced GSC increase (Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016; Uryu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016; Uryu et al., 2015) and confirmed by experiments in Figure 3.

claim: c587-GAL4–mediated Oamb knock-down significantly impaired mating-induced GSC increase.
source: In contrast, c587-GAL4–mediated Oamb knock-down (c587 >OambRNAi) showed significantly impaired mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing virgin and mated females with Oamb RNAi.

claim: The Oamb phenotype was observed with two independent UAS-Oamb-RNAi strains targeting different regions in the Oamb mRNA.
source: This phenotype was observed with two independent UAS-Oamb-RNAi strains (OambRNAi1 and OambRNAi2) (Figure 1C), each of which targeted a different region in the Oamb mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1C using two independent RNAi lines.

claim: Transgenic RNAi of other octopamine receptor genes (Octβ1R, Octβ2R and Octβ3R) had no significant effect on GSC number between virgin and mated females.
source: The specificity of Oamb was also confirmed by the fact that the c587-GAL4–driven transgenic RNAi of other octopamine receptor genes (Octβ1R, Octβ2R and Octβ3R) (Ohhara et al., 2012) had no significant effect on the GSC number between virgin and mated females (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1C and cited reference (Ohhara et al., 2012).

claim: Oamb has a pivotal role in mating-induced GSC increase.
source: Therefore, Oamb has a pivotal role in mating-induced GSC increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including RNAi knockdown and genetic mutant analysis.

claim: Oamb in mature follicle cells has a significant role in ovulation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that Oamb in mature follicle cells and in the oviduct has a significant role in ovulation (Deady and Sun, 2015; Lee et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Deady and Sun, 2015; Lee et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: Oamb in the oviduct has a significant role in ovulation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that Oamb in mature follicle cells and in the oviduct has a significant role in ovulation (Deady and Sun, 2015; Lee et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Deady and Sun, 2015; Lee et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: Mating-induced GSC increase was not impaired by Oamb RNAi in stage-14 follicle cells.
source: However, mating-induced GSC increase was not impaired by Oamb RNAi in the stage-14 follicle cells by R44E10-GAL4 (Deady and Sun, 2015) (R44E10 >OambRNAi), in the stage 9–10 follicle cells by c355-GAL4, c306-GAL4, and slbo-GAL4 (Barth et al., 2012), or in the common oviduct by RS-GAL4 (Lee et al., 2003) (RS >OambRNAi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and E with citations to previous work (Deady and Sun, 2015; Barth et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: Mating-induced GSC increase is independent from the ovulation process.
source: These data suggest that mating-induced GSC increase is independent from the ovulation process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Oamb RNAi in ovulation-related tissues does not affect GSC increase.

claim: Oamb RNAi in the nervous system did not affect mating-induced GSC increase.
source: However, Oamb RNAi in the nervous system (nSyb >OambRNAi) did not affect the mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the impairment of GSC increase of c587 >OambRNAi or tj >OambRNAi is not due to gene knock-down in neuronal cells but rather in the ovarian-somatic cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Oamb homozygous mutant females did not exhibit mating-induced GSC increase.
source: Similar to Oamb RNAi females, Oamb homozygous mutant females (c587>+; OambΔ/OambΔ) did not exhibit mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D using CRISPR/Cas9-generated Oamb mutants.

claim: The GSC increase of OambΔ/OambΔ was restored by overexpression of Oamb in the escort cells.
source: In addition, the GSC increase of OambΔ/OambΔ was restored by overexpression of Oamb in the escort cells (c587 >OambAS; OambΔ/OambΔ).
evidence: This is a rescue experiment demonstrating specificity of the Oamb mutation.

claim: Oamb in escort cells modulates GSC increase after mating.
source: These findings are all consistent with the idea that Oamb in escort cells modulates GSC increase after mating.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including RNAi, mutant analysis, and rescue experiments.

claim: Mating increased the frequency of GSCs in the M phase in control female flies.
source: In control female flies, mating increased the frequency of GSCs in the M phase (Figure 1E), whereas in c587 >OambRNAi flies, this was not observed.
evidence: Demonstrated by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In c587 >OambRNAi flies, mating did not increase the frequency of GSCs in the M phase.
source: In control female flies, mating increased the frequency of GSCs in the M phase (Figure 1E), whereas in c587 >OambRNAi flies, this was not observed.
evidence: Demonstrated by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The number of apoptotic cells in the germarium did not change in c587 >OambRNAi female flies compared with controls.
source: The number of apoptotic cells in the germarium did not change in c587 >OambRNAi female flies compared with controls (Figure 1F), suggesting that Oamb activates GSC increase by pushing the cell cycle of GSCs and that the lack of mating-induced GSC increase in Oamb RNAi is not due to the enhancement of cell death.
evidence: Demonstrated by Dcp-1 staining data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Oamb activates GSC increase by pushing the cell cycle of GSCs.
source: The number of apoptotic cells in the germarium did not change in c587 >OambRNAi female flies compared with controls (Figure 1F), suggesting that Oamb activates GSC increase by pushing the cell cycle of GSCs and that the lack of mating-induced GSC increase in Oamb RNAi is not due to the enhancement of cell death.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Oamb affects cell cycle but not apoptosis.

claim: The lack of mating-induced GSC increase in Oamb RNAi is not due to the enhancement of cell death.
source: The number of apoptotic cells in the germarium did not change in c587 >OambRNAi female flies compared with controls (Figure 1F), suggesting that Oamb activates GSC increase by pushing the cell cycle of GSCs and that the lack of mating-induced GSC increase in Oamb RNAi is not due to the enhancement of cell death.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the apoptosis data in Figure 1F.

claim: Mating-induced GSC increase is mediated by GSC niche signals.
source: Our previous studies revealed that mating-induced GSC increase is mediated by GSC niche signals (Ameku et al., 2018; Ameku and Niwa, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Ameku et al., 2018; Ameku and Niwa, 2016).

claim: Decapentaplegic (Dpp), the fly counterpart to bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), is the essential niche signal.
source: In particular, Decapentaplegic (Dpp), the fly counterpart to bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), is the essential niche signal (Spradling et al., 2011; Xie and Spradling, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Spradling et al., 2011; Xie and Spradling, 1998).

claim: Mating induced the increase in pMad level in GSCs.
source: We confirmed that mating induced the increase in pMad level in GSCs, whereas mating did not increase pMad levels in c587 >OambRNAi animals (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by pMad immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Mating did not increase pMad levels in c587 >OambRNAi animals.
source: We confirmed that mating induced the increase in pMad level in GSCs, whereas mating did not increase pMad levels in c587 >OambRNAi animals (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by pMad immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Mating increased the signal intensity of Dad-LacZ in GSCs.
source: We also confirmed that mating increased the signal intensity of Daughters against dpp (Dad)-LacZ, a reporter gene that reflect an expression of the BMP target gene Dad, while Oamb knock-down in the escort cells impaired the increase of Dad-LacZ signal after mating (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Dad-LacZ reporter data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Oamb knock-down in the escort cells impaired the increase of Dad-LacZ signal after mating.
source: We also confirmed that mating increased the signal intensity of Daughters against dpp (Dad)-LacZ, a reporter gene that reflect an expression of the BMP target gene Dad, while Oamb knock-down in the escort cells impaired the increase of Dad-LacZ signal after mating (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Dad-LacZ reporter data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Mating activates the BMP signal in GSCs through Oamb in the escort cells.
source: These results suggest that mating activates the BMP signal in GSCs through Oamb in the escort cells, thereby resulting in the increase in GSCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pMad and Dad-LacZ data.

claim: c587 >OambRNAi did not change the number of cap cells in virgin nor mated female flies.
source: c587 >OambRNAi did not change the number of cap cells in virgin nor mated female flies, suggesting that Oamb knock-down does not affect the overall architecture of the niche (Figure 1I).
evidence: Demonstrated by cap cell counting data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Oamb knock-down does not affect the overall architecture of the niche.
source: c587 >OambRNAi did not change the number of cap cells in virgin nor mated female flies, suggesting that Oamb knock-down does not affect the overall architecture of the niche (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cap cell counting data.

claim: Ovaries cultured with OA had more GSCs compared to those without OA after 12 hr incubation.
source: After incubation for 12 hr, the ovaries cultured with OA had more GSCs as compared to those without OA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The minimal OA concentration to induce ex vivo GSC increase was 1 μM.
source: Whereas the minimal OA concentration to induce ex vivo GSC increase was 1 μM, hereafter we used 100 μM OA because the GSC number plateaued with this concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: OA-mediated ex vivo GSC increase was not observed in c587 >OambRNAi virgin ovaries.
source: This OA-mediated ex vivo GSC increase was not observed in c587 >OambRNAi virgin ovaries (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: OA treatment was sufficient to induce the increase in pMad level in GSCs in ex vivo culture.
source: We confirmed that OA treatment was sufficient to induce the increase in pMad level in GSCs, even in the ex vivo culture system (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pMad immunostaining data in ex vivo cultured ovaries shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OA treatment did not increase pMad levels in c587 >OambRNAi ovaries.
source: On the other hand, OA treatment did not increase pMad levels in c587 >OambRNAi ovaries (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pMad immunostaining data in ex vivo cultured ovaries shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OA activates the BMP signal in GSCs through Oamb in the escort cells.
source: These results suggest that OA activates the BMP signal in GSCs through Oamb in the escort cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ex vivo OA treatment and pMad data.

claim: Upon OA binding, Oamb evokes Ca2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) into the cytosol, leading to a transient increase in intercellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i).
source: Upon OA binding, Oamb evokes Ca2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) into the cytosol, leading to a transient increase in intercellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) (Han et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Han et al., 1998).

claim: 100 μM of OA treatment evoked an increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence in the escort cells and follicle cells.
source: We found that 100 μM of OA treatment evoked an increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence in the escort cells and follicle cells, whereas the control medium treatment (0 μM of OA) did not show any increase in fluorescence (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; also see Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Control medium treatment (0 μM of OA) did not show any increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence.
source: We found that 100 μM of OA treatment evoked an increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence in the escort cells and follicle cells, whereas the control medium treatment (0 μM of OA) did not show any increase in fluorescence (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; also see Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The OA-mediated increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence intensity was not observed in the germarium of Oamb RNAi flies.
source: In addition, the OA-mediated increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence intensity was not observed in the germarium of Oamb RNAi flies (Figure 2E), suggesting that the OA-dependent increase in [Ca2+]i in the germarium is required for Oamb.
evidence: Demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The OA-dependent increase in [Ca2+]i in the germarium is required for Oamb.
source: In addition, the OA-mediated increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence intensity was not observed in the germarium of Oamb RNAi flies (Figure 2E), suggesting that the OA-dependent increase in [Ca2+]i in the germarium is required for Oamb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the calcium imaging data in Oamb RNAi flies.

claim: Irradiation of orange-light to c587-GAL4, nSyb-GAL80 >CsChrimson flies induced GSC increase in virgin females.
source: When we irradiated an orange-light to c587-GAL4, nSyb-GAL80 >CsChrimson flies to induce Ca2+ flux in the germarium (Figure 2F), GSC increased in the virgin females (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The ratio of GSC in the M phase increased by CsChrimson activation.
source: In addition, the ratio of GSC in the M phase increased by CsChrimson activation (Figure 2H).
evidence: Demonstrated by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The pMad level in GSCs was increased by CsChrimson activation.
source: Moreover, the pMad level in GSCs was increased by CsChrimson activation, suggesting that the forced Ca2+ flux is sufficient to induce GSC increase through the upregulation of BMP signaling (Figure 2I).
evidence: Demonstrated by pMad immunostaining data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Forced Ca2+ flux is sufficient to induce GSC increase through the upregulation of BMP signaling.
source: Moreover, the pMad level in GSCs was increased by CsChrimson activation, suggesting that the forced Ca2+ flux is sufficient to induce GSC increase through the upregulation of BMP signaling (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CsChrimson activation and pMad data.

claim: The knock-down of Insp3R suppressed GSC increase in mated females.
source: The knock-down of Inositol 3-receptor (c587 >Insp3RRNAi) encoding a protein that releases the stored Ca2+ from ER suppressed GSC increase in mated females (Figure 2J).
evidence: Demonstrated by Insp3R RNAi data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The overexpression of Insp3R in the escort cells increased the GSC number in virgin females.
source: Conversely, the overexpression of Insp3R in the escort cells increased the GSC number in virgin females (Figure 2J).
evidence: Demonstrated by Insp3R overexpression data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: OA-mediated ex vivo GSC increase was not observed in c587 >Insp3RRNAi virgin ovaries.
source: Furthermore, OA-mediated ex vivo GSC increase was not observed in c587 >Insp3RRNAi virgin ovaries (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: OA signaling regulates the mating-induced GSC increase by controlling Ca2+ signaling in escort cells.
source: Overall, we demonstrated that OA signaling regulates the mating-induced GSC increase by controlling Ca2+ signaling in escort cells, which is thereby necessary and sufficient to induce GSC increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including calcium imaging, optogenetics, and Insp3R manipulation.

claim: Ca2+ signaling in escort cells is necessary and sufficient to induce GSC increase.
source: Overall, we demonstrated that OA signaling regulates the mating-induced GSC increase by controlling Ca2+ signaling in escort cells, which is thereby necessary and sufficient to induce GSC increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including calcium imaging, optogenetics, and Insp3R manipulation.

claim: The biosynthesis and signaling of ecdysteroid in the ovary are required for the mating-induced GSC increase.
source: The biosynthesis and signaling of ecdysteroid in the ovary are required for the mating-induced GSC increase (Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016).

claim: The RNAi of neverland (nvd) in the escort cells suppressed the mating-induced GSC increase.
source: As we have previously reported, the RNAi of neverland (nvd), which encodes an ecdysteroidogenic enzyme (Yoshiyama-Yanagawa et al., 2011; Yoshiyama et al., 2006) in the escort cells, suppressed the mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 3A; Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated by nvd RNAi data shown in Figure 3A with citations to previous work (Yoshiyama-Yanagawa et al., 2011; Yoshiyama et al., 2006; Ameku et al., 2017; Ameku and Niwa, 2016).

claim: The RNAi of ecdysone receptor (EcR) in the escort cells suppressed the mating-induced GSC increase.
source: We also found a similar phenotype in the RNAi of ecdysone receptor (EcR) in the escort cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by EcR RNAi data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The OA-mediated GSC increase was not observed in nvd RNAi ovaries.
source: Interestingly, the OA-mediated GSC increase was not observed in nvd RNAi ovaries (c587 >nvdRNAi) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The impairment of GSC increase in c587 >nvdRNAi was restored with the administration of 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) in the culture media.
source: Moreover, this impairment of GSC increase in c587 >nvdRNAi was restored with the administration of 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) in the culture media.
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data with 20E supplementation shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 20E treatment without OA did not induce GSC increase in the control ovaries.
source: On the other hand, 20E treatment without OA did not induce GSC increase in the control ovaries (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wild-type virgin females fed with 20E did not exhibit any increase in GSCs.
source: This observation is consistent with our previous study showing that wild-type virgin females fed with 20E did not exhibit any increase in GSCs (Ameku and Niwa, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ameku and Niwa, 2016).

claim: 20E is required for the OA-mediated increase in GSCs.
source: Therefore, 20E is required for the OA-mediated increase in GSCs; however, by itself, 20E is not sufficient to induce GSC increase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ex vivo culture experiments with OA and 20E.

claim: 20E by itself is not sufficient to induce GSC increase.
source: Therefore, 20E is required for the OA-mediated increase in GSCs; however, by itself, 20E is not sufficient to induce GSC increase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ex vivo culture experiments with OA and 20E.

claim: At a restrictive temperature of 31°C, the mating-induced GSC increase was suppressed in EcRA483T/EcRM54fs flies.
source: At a restrictive temperature of 31°C, the mating-induced GSC increase was suppressed in EcRA483T/EcRM54fs flies, consistent with our previous report (Ameku and Niwa, 2016; Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by temperature-shift experiment data shown in Figure 3C with citation to previous work (Ameku and Niwa, 2016).

claim: The OA-dependent GSC increase was suppressed in EcRA483T/EcRM54fs ovaries in ex vivo experiment.
source: In the ex vivo experiment, the OA-dependent GSC increase was also suppressed in EcRA483T/EcRM54fs ovaries (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: OA-Oamb-Ca2+ signaling requires ovarian ecdysteroid signaling.
source: These results suggest that OA-Oamb-Ca2+ signaling requires ovarian ecdysteroid signaling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experiments with nvd and EcR mutants.

claim: OA-Oamb-Ca2+ signaling and ecdysteroid biosynthesis are essential in the follicle rupture in D. melanogaster ovary.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have reported that they are also essential in the follicle rupture in D. melanogaster ovary (Deady and Sun, 2015; Knapp and Sun, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Deady and Sun, 2015; Knapp and Sun, 2017).

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase 2 (Mmp2) acts downstream of the OA-Oamb-Ca2+ signaling pathway in mature follicle cells.
source: In this process, Matrix metalloproteinase 2 (Mmp2), a membrane-conjugated proteinase, acts downstream of the OA-Oamb-Ca2+ signaling pathway in mature follicle cells (Deady et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Deady et al., 2015).

claim: Mmp2 is expressed in niche cells, including escort cells.
source: Because recent studies have indicated the expression of Mmp2 in niche cells, including escort cells (Pearson et al., 2016; Wang and Page-McCaw, 2014), we examined Mmp2 function in the escort cells using RNAi of Mmp2 with c587-GAL4.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Pearson et al., 2016; Wang and Page-McCaw, 2014).

claim: c587 >Mmp2RNAi impaired mating-induced GSC increase.
source: Similar to c587 >OambRNAi, c587 >Mmp2RNAi impaired mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Mmp2 RNAi data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mmp2 knock-down in cap cells by bab-GAL4 suppressed GSC increase.
source: Notably, Mmp2 knock-down in cap cells by bab-GAL4 also suppressed GSC increase, suggesting that Mmp2 acts in both escort cells and cap cells to induce GSC increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Mmp2 RNAi data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mmp2 acts in both escort cells and cap cells to induce GSC increase.
source: Notably, Mmp2 knock-down in cap cells by bab-GAL4 also suppressed GSC increase, suggesting that Mmp2 acts in both escort cells and cap cells to induce GSC increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Mmp2 RNAi data in different cell types.

claim: Mmp2 RNAi in the ovarian-somatic cells by Tj-GAL4 resulted in the failure of mating-induced GSC increase.
source: We also found that Mmp2 RNAi in the ovarian-somatic cells by another GAL4 (Tj >Mmp2RNAi1) resulted in the failure of mating-induced GSC increase, whereas Mmp2 RNAi in the nervous system (nSyb >Mmp2RNAi1) and in the follicle cells of stage 14 oocytes (R44E10 >Mmp2RNAi1) had no effect on GSC increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Mmp2 RNAi data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mmp2 RNAi in the nervous system had no effect on GSC increase.
source: We also found that Mmp2 RNAi in the ovarian-somatic cells by another GAL4 (Tj >Mmp2RNAi1) resulted in the failure of mating-induced GSC increase, whereas Mmp2 RNAi in the nervous system (nSyb >Mmp2RNAi1) and in the follicle cells of stage 14 oocytes (R44E10 >Mmp2RNAi1) had no effect on GSC increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Mmp2 RNAi data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mmp2 RNAi in the follicle cells of stage 14 oocytes had no effect on GSC increase.
source: We also found that Mmp2 RNAi in the ovarian-somatic cells by another GAL4 (Tj >Mmp2RNAi1) resulted in the failure of mating-induced GSC increase, whereas Mmp2 RNAi in the nervous system (nSyb >Mmp2RNAi1) and in the follicle cells of stage 14 oocytes (R44E10 >Mmp2RNAi1) had no effect on GSC increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Mmp2 RNAi data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mmp2 in the escort cells and cap cells are necessary to induce post-mating GSC increase.
source: These results suggest that Mmp2 in the escort cells and cap cells are necessary to induce post-mating GSC increase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Mmp2 RNAi data in different cell types.

claim: Timp encodes an endogenous proteinase inhibitor of Mmp2.
source: In the GSC niche cells in D. melanogaster, Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (Timp) gene encoding an endogenous proteinase inhibitor of Mmp2 is expressed (Gomis-Rüth et al., 1997; Page-McCaw et al., 2003; Pearson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Gomis-Rüth et al., 1997; Page-McCaw et al., 2003; Pearson et al., 2016).

claim: The knock-down of Timp in escort cells induced GSC increase even in virgin females.
source: The knock-down of Timp in escort cells induced GSC increase even in virgin females, whereas its overexpression suppressed mating-induced GSC increase (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Timp RNAi and overexpression data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Timp overexpression suppressed mating-induced GSC increase.

evidence: Demonstrated by TRIC calcium reporter data shown in Figure 5I–L.

evidence: This is speculation based on previous work (Knapp and Sun, 2017).

source: In female D. melanogaster, several post-mating responses are coordinated by SPSNs and their downstream afferent neuronal circuit (Wang et al., 2020), including Stato-Acoustic Ganglion neurons, the ventral abdominal lateral Myoinhibitory peptide neurons, and the efferent dsx+ Tdc2+ neurons (Feng et al., 2014; Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Jang et al., 2017; Rezával et al., 2014).
